'''James Alexander Mackay''' (21 November 1936 – 12 August 2007) was a prolific Scottish writer and [[Philately|philatelist]] whose output of philatelic works was rivalled only by [[Fred Melville]].{{Citation needed|date=September 2011}} He was described by [[John R. Holman|John Holman]], editor of the ''[[British Philatelic Bulletin]]'', as a "philatelic writer without equal"<ref>''Gibbons Stamp Monthly'', October 2007.</ref> but his reputation was damaged by a conviction for theft from the British Museum early in his career, which cost him his job there, and multiple accusations of plagiarism.

== Early life and family ==
James Mackay was born in Inverness on 21 November 1936. He was educated in Glasgow, where he also attended the university. Later in life Mackay was awarded a Doctor of Literature (D.Litt.) degree by [[Glasgow University]].

He married Renate.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20110929134902/http://www.gbstamps.com/gbcc/gbcc_mackay_intvw.html "In The Spotlight"], Great Britain Collectors Club, 1999. Retrieved 25 October 2017. Archived at webcitation.org.</ref>

== Scottish posts ==
Interested in [[Postage stamps|stamps]] and the [[postal system]] from an early age, he wrote two acclaimed histories of the Scottish posts; one limited to [[St. Kilda, Scotland|St. Kilda]] and, in 1978, his ''History of Scottish Postmarks, 1693–1978'', the definitive work on the subject. He became a prolific philatelic author, especially on English, Irish and Scottish [[postmark]]s and also produced popular Postal History Annuals and island series books. He wrote some 200 books and at least 10,000 articles. Mackay's interest in the postal history of St Kilda had been formed during his time stationed there during his army service in the 1950s.

== Theft from the British Museum ==
In 1972 Mackay was dismissed from his job as an assistant keeper at the [[British Library Philatelic Collections|British Museum]] in London after he was convicted at the [[Old Bailey]] of stealing valuable proof stamps.<ref>"Writer in disgrace as book halted by publisher" Stephen Breen & Catherine Lockerbie, ''The Scotsman''.</ref> He had pleaded guilty to five charges of stealing progressive proofs on loan from the [[Crown Agents Philatelic and Security Printing Archive|Crown Agents]] from the Museum in 1965 and 1966 and was fined £1000. He had exchanged the proofs with dealer [[Clive Feigenbaum]] for Winston Churchill-themed stamps.<ref>"Stamp expert fined for thefts from museum" in ''The Times'', 6 September 1972, p.3.</ref>

== Writing ==
He was the editor of ''The Burns Chronicle'' from 1976 to 1992, which under his stewardship reached a level of quality and diversity it has not achieved before or since.{{citation needed|date=October 2017}} He then turned to biography, where he was less successful. Through the 1980s he worked on a biography of [[Robert Burns]] which was published in 1992 to favourable reviews and which won the [[Saltire Society Literary Awards|Saltire Society Book of the Year Award]]. Subsequent biographies of [[Allan Pinkerton]] and [[William Wallace]] received more mixed reviews.

1996 saw the release of ''[[Michael Collins (Irish leader)|Michael Collins: A Life]]'', a work about the life of the famed Irish revolutionary which received excellent reviews.

Mackay also wrote books under a number of different pseudonyms, including Ian Angus, William Finlay, Bruce Garden, Alex Matheson and Peter Whittington.<ref>[http://www.trussel.com/books/pseud_m.htm Author Pseudonyms]</ref><ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=phhhHT64kIMC&dq=stamps%20%22Peter%20Whittington&pg=PA356 International Who's Who of Authors, 2004, p.356]</ref>

==Accusations of plagiarism==
In 1998, he published a biography of [[Alexander Graham Bell]]. It was on the market briefly before [[Robert V. Bruce]] published a damning indictment, detailing sustained [[plagiarism]] of his own work, ''Alexander Graham Bell and the Conquest of Solitude''. Far from being a little-known work, the latter had in fact been nominated for the [[Pulitzer Prize]] in 1973. The indictment, published in the [[American Historical Association]]'s house journal, counted instances of plagiarism on 80 per cent of the pages published. Mackay paid his publishers to withdraw the book from circulation, and Bruce agreed not to sue.<ref>{{cite news |last=Blumenthal |first=Ralph |author2=Lyall, Sarah |title=Repeat Accusations of Plagiarism Taint Prolific Biographer |series=Sunday Book Review |work=[[The New York Times]]|date=21 September 1999 |url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9B04E0DB1F3CF932A1575AC0A96F958260 |accessdate=10 March 2011 }}</ref><ref>Robert V. Bruce in George Mason University's History News Network http://hnn.us/articles/633.html</ref>

Mackay then published a biography of [[John Paul Jones]], the founder of the [[US Navy]]. While initially well received, and the subject of flattering reviews in the trade press, it was soon discovered that it was practically a copy of what those same reviews had marked as the last work on the man, that by [[Samuel Eliot Morison]] in 1942. That biography too had won the Pulitzer. Columbia University history professor [[David Armitage (historian)|David Armitage]] was quoted in the ''[[New York Times]]'' as saying that the book was "a spectacular and sustained act of plagiarism."<ref>New York Times 25 Sep 1999 "Publisher Cancels Biography After Plagiarism Inquiry" [https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9B07E0D8133FF936A1575AC0A96F958260] retrieved on 9 Nov 2007</ref><ref>[[Scotland on Sunday]] "Muckle 'o grief as expert on the bard reviles 'plagiarist'" [http://scotlandonsunday.scotsman.com/index.cfm?id=1597732001] retrieved on 9 November 2007.</ref>

Despite these accusations, Mackay continued to be commissioned to write articles for the philatelic press, and it has been said that almost the entire text of some editions of ''Stamp & Coin Mart'', a popular British magazine, were written by him.

== Death ==
Mackay died on 12 August 2007 at the age of 70 in Glasgow.<ref>[http://news.scotsman.com/obituaries.cfm?id=1343062007 Prolific writer on philatelic subjects and biographer of Burns] Scotsman.com (retrieved 4 November 2007)</ref>
